title: Most Language Models can be Poets too: An AI Writing Assistant and Constrained Text Generation Studio
venue: Proceedings of the 2nd Workshop on When Creative AI Meets Conversational AI (CAI2), COLING 2022
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of constrained natural language generation: how to make language models produce text that obeys hard lexical, semantic, or phonetic constraints, such as banning a letter, matching a syllable count, or satisfying rhyme-related properties. The authors argue that while large language models are strong generators, prior work has paid limited attention to simple, plug-and-play ways of enforcing these kinds of token-level constraints during decoding. They position the work mainly as a creative writing and research tool rather than as an educational intervention study.

The core approach is to filter a language model’s vocabulary before each token is generated, compositionally applying user-specified constraints without retraining or modifying the underlying model. To demonstrate this, the paper introduces Constrained Text Generation Studio (CTGS), a graphical AI writing assistant, and a Hugging Face web app called Gadsby. The system supports a wide range of lexical, semantic, and phonetic filters, including banning specific letters, forcing letter inclusion, semantic similarity thresholds, syllable count, meter, rhyme, and phonetic matching. The paper also introduces a new constrained-writing dataset, Lipogram-e, composed of book-length English texts omitting the letter “e.”

No K-12, higher education, or other human participant population is empirically studied. The paper discusses possible users such as poets, creative writers, recreational linguists, and researchers, but does not report a formal user study, educational deployment, or participant sample. Its empirical component is instead a technical evaluation using GPT-2-medium on the Lipogram-e dataset, comparing base, fine-tuned, and over-fine-tuned models with and without the vocabulary constraint filter.

The main conclusion is that vocabulary filtering can effectively enforce hard constraints while preserving usable text generation, and on the Lipogram-e benchmark it yields strictly better performance than fine-tuning alone: lower perplexity and zero ignored-constraint errors across tested conditions. The authors also note important caveats, including degenerate generation behavior under heavy filtering and limitations caused by subword tokenization. Overall, the paper is best understood as a technical systems and methods contribution, not a direct education study and not direct evidence for K-12 literacy impacts of generative AI.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a workshop technical paper evaluating model behavior, not a K-12 education study. It provides no learner sample, no educational study design, and no causal evidence about student outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows technical performance improvements for constrained text generation, but educational impact is unclear because no K-12 learners, teachers, or direct learning outcomes were studied.

interventions.use_case: Constrained text generation writing assistant (CTGS/Gadsby) that helps users generate or manually select creative writing continuations under lexical, semantic, and phonetic constraints such as banning letters, enforcing syllable counts, rhyme, or meter.

finding.finding_summary: In a technical evaluation on the Lipogram-e dataset, applying vocabulary-level constraint filters to GPT-2 variants reduced perplexity relative to the same models without filters and eliminated ignored-constraint errors. Reported results were GPT-2 perplexity 237.37 vs 211.53 with filter, GPT-2 fine-tuned 5 epochs 78.24 vs 77.99 with filter, and GPT-2 fine-tuned 20 epochs 75.58 vs 75.10 with filter; ignored constraint error rates fell from 28.2%, 0.5%, and 0.3% respectively to 0%.
finding.measure: Language-model perplexity on test split; ignored constraint error percentage on Lipogram-e dataset
